title_en: Will we still work five days a week?
topic: work and employment 工作与就业
paras: Predictions about work are as old as work itself. A century ago, economists promised that machines would cut the working week to fifteen hours; in the 1970s, futurologists said robots would take over all the repetitive jobs while we relaxed by the pool. None of it happened. Today the forecasts are bolder: Elon Musk has suggested that artificial intelligence will eventually mean nobody has to work, and that the nine-to-five job is finished for good. After Covid, millions of people were pushed out of the office and into the spare room, which made the daily commute look very old-fashioned. So should we believe the new predictions?

Professor Brendan Burchell, a sociologist at Cambridge, takes such claims with a large pinch of salt. He points out that the track record of economists is poor: for a hundred years they have predicted dramatic reductions in working time, and those predictions simply have not come to pass. Hours do fall, he says, but slowly, in small steps. To be sceptical, in other words, is not to be gloomy — it is simply to notice how often the future arrives late.

The bigger danger, then, may not be mass unemployment but bad timing. Andrew Palmer, business editor of The Economist, says he is no dystopian and does not believe that machines will get rid of every job. His worry is a sequencing risk: some professions will be disrupted long before the new jobs crop up, and the two will not necessarily be aligned. This mismatch, he argues, is where the damage is done. A worker who loses a role at forty-five cannot wait for a job that has not been invented yet. Retraining and a decent safety net matter far more than any forecast.

One change, at least, is already being tested. In 2023, sixty British companies tried a four-day week on full pay. When the trial ended, 92% of them chose to keep it — not only because staff were happier, but because productivity held up and fewer people resigned. Shorter hours, in other words, did not mean less output. The lesson is not that a three-day weekend is inevitable; it is that we can choose which parts of the future to adopt. Flexible arrangements and a better work-life balance are not science fiction. They are decisions that companies are making right now.
vocab: 反乌托邦的；极度悲观的

title_en: What we lose when we scroll
title_zh: 刷掉无聊，我们丢了什么？
topic: psychology and attention 心理与注意力
paras: Not long ago, boredom was a problem waiting to be solved. Machines, they promised, would fill every dull hour, and when the smartphone arrived the promise seemed kept. Today a spare moment rarely stays spare. The queue at the bank, the bus stop, the four minutes before a lecture — screens now occupy all of them. Being bored, we are told, is simply bad time management. But is a life without boredom really an improvement?

Psychologists are not so sure. Dr Sandi Mann, who lectures in psychology at the University of Central Lancashire, argues that the cure may be feeding the disease. The more entertainment we surround ourselves with, the more bored we seem to become, because we grow addicted to stimulation and to novelty. Manoush Zomorodi, author and host of the Zig Zag podcast, adds a warning of her own. Mind-wandering, she points out, does not lead straight to brilliant ideas; first comes an uncomfortable stretch in which the mind turns to things we would rather avoid. Most of us retreat to the phone at exactly that moment.

This is where the real cost appears. When nothing is happening, the mind is free to drift, and drifting is how unrelated memories meet and new connections form. That is the raw material of problem-solving. Swiping and scrolling interrupt the process at its most fragile point: they offer relief before the dull phase has done its work. The word boredom carries a negative connotation for a simple reason — we remember the discomfort, not the ideas that followed it. We have built a machine for skipping the part that pays.

The evidence is not only anecdotal. In a widely cited experiment, Dr Mann and a colleague gave one group a deliberately dull task — copying numbers out of a telephone directory — while another group went straight to the test. Both were then asked to list unusual uses for a plastic cup. The bored volunteers produced more original answers. The lesson is not that we should stare at walls for hours; it is that boredom is better treated as an ingredient than as a fault. Mann's phrase for it: boredom is the mother of invention. A short walk without headphones may be the cheapest version of that idea.

It has no effect on attention
It should be banned for children
questions.why: The more entertainment we surround ourselves with, the more bored we seem to become。

questions.why: first comes an uncomfortable stretch in which the mind turns to things we would rather avoid。

title_en: Why learning a language shrinks your brain
title_zh: 学外语让语言区变小，为什么是好事？
topic: language and the brain 语言与大脑
paras: For years the message ran in one direction: the more languages you learn, the more brain you build. Parents were told that a second language would exercise the mind, and scientists expected to find the proof inside the skull. So when Eve Fedorenko, a neuroscientist at Harvard, began scanning children who already spoke several languages, her prediction was modest. Their language areas, she assumed, would be hyperactive — busier and larger than those of a child raised on one language alone.

The scans said otherwise. The language regions of the multilingual children were not larger; they were smaller. Fedorenko calls the result surprising, and the reason is easy to see. A smaller area sounds like a deficit, something taken away. Reports of the study reached for the same word: shrink. But a shrinking muscle and a shrinking language area are not the same story, and the difference is where the lesson sits.

What the scans measured was efficiency, not damage. As children reuse the patterns of a language, the work turns automatic: they no longer assemble a sentence word by word, and the brain quietly releases the tissue it no longer needs. Fedorenko puts it plainly — the more automatic a task becomes, the more the activation shrinks, because you need less brain tissue to do the job as well. Her point is not that the brain wears out. It is that this compression arrives only through repetition, and a learner who never repeats never earns it.

The evidence runs past the scanner. Frederique Liegeois, a cognitive neuroscientist at University College London, has found that bilingual adults with dementia tend to show symptoms later than those who speak a single language. The daily juggle of two systems seems to build a reserve that holds the line a little longer. Richard Simcot, who speaks eleven languages, says he learns them not because he needs them but for sheer enjoyment. That may be the useful conclusion for anyone facing an exam: a language is not a deposit you make once and forget. It is a habit that keeps the machine tuned.

questions.why: What the scans measured was efficiency, not damage。

questions.q: How does the brain achieve this compression?
questions.why: this compression arrives only through repetition。

title_en: Sleep is not a pause in your life
title_zh: 睡觉不是暂停，是大脑在上夜班
topic: sleep and memory 睡眠与记忆
paras: Evolution is supposed to reward good design, and sleep looks like a fault. Every night we lie down, lose consciousness and leave ourselves vulnerable for hours; an animal that slept like this in the open would have been eaten. The existence of sleep has therefore always been a puzzle. The comfortable answer was that the body shuts down to save energy — that the brain, like a laptop, goes into standby and does nothing until morning. If that were true, sleep would be a pause, and the sensible advice to a student with an exam tomorrow would be to stay up.

The evidence points the other way. Ginny Smith, a science journalist speaking on BBC Radio 4, describes the morning after a bad night: you cannot concentrate, and the brain is in no state to take in new information. The greater loss, though, comes after learning rather than before it. Sleep is when the brain consolidates what it has taken in, moving material out of short-term storage into what you already know. An old adage tells us to sleep on a difficult problem. Smith's claim is that the saying is literally true: the brain keeps working while you do not.

The mechanism behind the loss is stress. Deprivation — having too little of something the body needs — is read as a threat. It triggers the fight-or-flight response, which redirects the body's budget towards immediate survival and away from long-term repair. One bad night is recoverable. A chronic shortage is not, because such a response never stands down: the immune system is slowly undermined, and the damage arrives later, as heart disease rather than as a cough.

What makes the case convincing is the size of the effect. People who regularly get enough sleep live about five years longer than those who do not, and the average person passes a third of life asleep — some 229,000 hours. The old picture has the cause reversed: sleep is not the interval between useful hours but the shift in which the day's material is filed away. For a student, three hours of extra revision bought with three hours of lost sleep may cancel each other out; a full night is what restores the machine for the morning.

questions.why: lose consciousness and leave ourselves vulnerable for hours。
